competition: Portuguese Mathematical Olympiad (National Final, Category B)

problems.problem: Determine the smallest positive integer that has exactly $1994$ divisors.

In a square $ABCD$ consider a point $E$ on side $AB$, different from $A$ and $B$. On side $BC$ consider the point $F$ such that the angles $\angle AED$ and $\angle DEF$ are equal. Prove that $EF=AE+FC$.
Prove that for every positive integer $n$ the number $$\underbrace{11\cdots11}_{2n\text{ digits}}-\underbrace{22\cdots22}_{n\text{ digits}}$$ is a perfect square.

So far, in every Final of the Mathematical Olympiads, no participant has been able to solve all the problems, but every problem has been solved by at least one participant. Prove that in every Final there was a participant $A$ who solved a problem $P_A$ and another participant $B$ who solved a problem $P_B$ such that $A$ did not solve $P_B$ and $B$ did not solve $P_A$.

Consider a circle $\mathcal C$ with centre $O$ and a point $Q$ inside it, different from $O$. Where should a point $P$ be placed on $\mathcal C$ so that the angle $\angle OPQ$ is as large as possible?

João Jump-the-Puddles jumps $1$ metre in his first jump, $2$ metres in the second, $4$ metres in the third, $\dots$, $2^{n-1}$ metres in jump number $n$. Can João choose the directions of his jumps so that he returns to his starting point?

Through an informer, the police know the meeting place of a gang of criminals, but the identities of the members are unknown. Inspector Loureiro's task is to arrest the gang leader, who is known to be the shortest of the five members, all of different heights, who will attend the meeting. After the meeting the criminals, as a precaution, leave the building separately at intervals of $15$ minutes. Since the inspector does not know which of them is the shortest, he decides to let the first two criminals leave and then to arrest the first of the following ones who is shorter than all those who have left before him. What is the probability that Inspector Loureiro arrests the right person?

Three ants are at three of the vertices of a rectangle. Each ant moves only while the other two are standing still, and always parallel to the line through the other two. Is it possible for the three ants to be at the same time at midpoints of sides of the rectangle?

The diameter $[AC]$ of a circle is divided into four equal segments by the points $P$, $M$ and $Q$. Consider a segment $[BD]$ through $P$ meeting the circle at $B$ and $D$, such that $PD=\frac32AP$. Given that the area of triangle $[ABP]$ is $1$ cm$^2$, compute the area of the quadrilateral $[ABCD]$.

Rosa, Aurora and Manuela held a competition last weekend consisting of several athletics events. In each event the winner obtained $x$ points, the second $y$ points and the third $z$ points, where $x,y,z$ are positive integers with $x>y>z$. The final result, obtained by adding the points of all events, was: Rosa $22$ points, Manuela $9$ points, Aurora $9$ points. In how many events did they compete, and who came second in the high jump, given that Manuela won the $100$ metres and that nobody withdrew from any event?
Prove that a real number $x$ is rational if and only if the sequence $$x,\ x+1,\ x+2,\ x+3,\ \dots,\ x+n,\ \dots$$ contains at least three terms in geometric progression.

A square is constructed on the hypotenuse of a right triangle $[ABC]$ (right-angled at $B$). Show that the segment joining the vertex $B$ to the centre of the square makes angles of $45^\circ$ with both legs of the triangle.

Show that among any three positive numbers one can choose two, say $x$ and $y$ with $x>y$, such that $$\frac{x-y}{1+xy}<1.$$ Show moreover that if the number $1$ on the right-hand side is replaced by any smaller number, however close to $1$, the statement becomes false.

A box contains $900$ cards numbered from $100$ to $999$. Paulo draws some cards from the box at random and computes, for each card, the sum of its digits. How many cards must Paulo draw to be sure of finding at least three cards with the same digit sum?

Have you ever found it odd that ``almost equal'' numbers may look very different? For example, in the decimal system $29$ and $30$ differ by one unit but have no digit in common. The numeration system ALPHABETA uses only the digits $0$ and $1$ and avoids this situation: $$\begin{array}{c|ccccccccc}\text{Decimal}&0&1&2&3&4&5&6&7&8\\ \hline \text{ALPHABETA}&0&1&11&10&110&111&101&100&1100\end{array}$$ The rule for constructing the successor of a number is: without repeating an earlier number of the list, change the rightmost possible digit; if this is impossible, put a $1$ on the left.

(a) Which decimal number is represented in ALPHABETA by $111111$?

(b) What is the next number in this code?

(c) Describe an algorithm that, given any number in the ALPHABETA code, finds the next number in the code.

Consider a right isosceles triangle whose legs have length $1$ cm. Suppose each point of the triangle is assigned one of the colours brown, blue, green and orange. Prove that, however this is done, there are two points of the same colour at distance at least $2-\sqrt2$ cm from each other.

In a regular polygon with $134$ sides, $67$ diagonals are drawn so that exactly one diagonal leaves each vertex. The length of a diagonal is defined as the number of sides of the polygon between its endpoints that is at most $67$. Ordering the lengths of the diagonals increasingly gives a sequence of $67$ numbers $(d_1,d_2,\dots,d_{67})$. Is it possible to draw the diagonals so that

(a) $(d_1,\dots,d_{67})=(\underbrace{2,\dots,2}_{6},\underbrace{3,\dots,3}_{61})$?

(b) $(d_1,\dots,d_{67})=(\underbrace{3,\dots,3}_{8},\underbrace{6,\dots,6}_{55},\underbrace{8,\dots,8}_{4})$?

A test has twenty questions. Seven points are awarded for each correct answer, two points are deducted for each wrong answer, and no points are awarded or deducted for an unanswered question. Joana obtained $87$ points. How many questions did she leave unanswered?

Consider a cube $ABCDEFGH$ with faces $ABCD$ and $EFGH$ and edges $AE$, $BF$, $CG$, $DH$ (in the face $ABCD$, $AB$ and $CD$ are opposite edges). Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of $[AB]$ and $[CD]$ respectively. Let $P$ be a point on the line $AE$, and $Q$ the intersection of the lines $PM$ and $BF$. Prove that triangle $[PQN]$ is isosceles.

In the country of Abaliba there are twenty cities and two airlines, Blue Planes and Red Planes. Flights are planned as follows: for any two cities, exactly one of the two airlines operates direct flights (in both directions, without stops) between them. Moreover, there are two cities $A$ and $B$ between which it is not possible to fly (even with stops) using only Red Planes. Show that, for any two cities, a passenger can travel from one to the other using only Blue Planes with at most one stop in a third city.

The dodo was a strange animal. Since it is extinct, one can only conjecture about its way of life. One of the most peculiar conjectures concerns the way the dodo moved: an adult apparently moved only by jumps of two types:

- type I: $1$ metre east and $3$ metres north;

- type II: $2$ metres west and $4$ metres south.

(a) Show that the dodo could reach a point $19$ metres east and $95$ metres north of it, and determine the number of jumps of each type it needed.

(b) Show that the dodo could not reach a point $18$ metres east and $95$ metres north of it.

A square region of side $12$ contains a water source supplying an irrigation system made of several straight channels forming polygonal lines. Regard the source as a point and each channel as a line segment. A point is irrigated if it is at distance at most $1$ from some channel, and the system was designed so that the whole region is irrigated. Prove that the total length of the irrigation channels exceeds $70$.

$n$ parallel lines of lengths $a_1\le a_2\le a_3\le\cdots\le a_n$ were painted to mark an airport hall. The architect then decided that the $n$ lines should all have equal length. If the cost per metre of extending a line equals the cost per metre of shortening it, what common length should the lines have so that the cost is minimal?

A chicken breeder wanted to check the price per chick he had charged the year before. He found a half-erased invoice reading: ``$72$ chicks sold for $*679*$ escudos'' (the units digit and the ten-thousands digit were illegible). At what price had he sold each chick the year before?
A regular octagon $ABCDEFGH$ is inscribed in a circle of radius $1$, and $P$ is an arbitrary point of this circle. Compute $$PA^2+PB^2+\cdots+PH^2.$$
Can the set $\{1,2,3,\dots,3000\}$ contain a subset of $2000$ elements none of which is twice another?
What is the greatest integer less than or equal to $$\frac{3^{31}+2^{31}}{3^{29}+2^{29}}\ ?$$

The points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ lie on a circle in this order, so that the arc $AB$ not containing $C$ and the arc $BD$ containing $C$ have the same length. $M$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $B$ to the segment $[AC]$. Prove that $AM=CD+CM$.
Let $a_0$ be a positive real number and consider the sequence defined by $$a_n=a_{n-1}+\frac1{a_{n-1}},\qquad n=1,2,3,\dots$$ Show that $a_{1998}>63$.
A number is called balanced if one of its digits is the mean of the others. How many balanced three-digit numbers are there?
How many positive integers $n$ are there such that $$\frac{2n^2+4n+18}{3n+3}$$ is an integer?
Two parallel chords of a circle, of lengths $10$ mm and $14$ mm, are $6$ mm apart. How long is the chord equidistant from them?

Given a number, we compute its square and add $1$ to the sum of the digits of this square, obtaining a new number. Starting with the number $7$ we obtain in the first step the number $1+(4+9)=14$, since $7^2=49$. Which number do we obtain in the $1999$th step?
Each of the numbers $a_1,\dots,a_n$ equals $1$ or $-1$. Prove that if $$a_1a_2+a_2a_3+\cdots+a_{n-1}a_n+a_na_1=0,$$ then $n$ is divisible by $4$.

In triangle $[ABC]$, $D$ is the midpoint of $[AB]$ and $E$ is the point of trisection of $[BC]$ closest to $C$. If the angles $\angle ADC$ and $\angle BAE$ are equal, how large is the angle $\angle BAC$?

Consider a $3\times 3$ table in which initially all cells contain zeros. The table may be changed by the following operation: choose a $2\times 2$ square formed by adjacent cells and add $1$ to all its numbers. Complete the following table, knowing that it was obtained by a sequence of allowed operations: $$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}\hline 14&&\\ \hline 19&36&\\ \hline &16&\\ \hline\end{array}$$

The chord $[CD]$ of a circle is perpendicular to the diameter $[AB]$ and meets it at $H$. The length $AB$ is a two-digit positive integer; reversing the order of its two digits gives the length $CD$. Knowing that the distance from $H$ to the centre $O$ is a positive rational number, compute $AB$.
For each positive integer $n$, determine the largest positive integer $k$ such that $2^k$ divides $3^n+1$.
Compute the sum of all the numbers that can be formed using each of the odd digits exactly once, that is, of the numbers $13579, 13597, \dots, 97531$.

In triangle $[ABC]$ the angle at $B$ is right; $E$ is a point of $[AB]$ and $D$ a point of $[AC]$ such that triangle $[DEC]$ has a right angle at $D$. Given that $EB=\frac12$, $EC=1$ and $AD=1$, compute $DC$.

$n$ players take part in a tournament. Each player plays each other player exactly once, and there are no draws. A player $A$ is called a champion if for every other player $B$ one of the following holds: (a) $A$ beat $B$; (b) $A$ beat a player $C$ who in turn beat $B$. Show that such a tournament cannot have exactly two champions.

To play the Game of the Goose, seven friends have to form four teams, which of course need not have the same number of members. In how many different ways can they form these teams? (The order of the people within a team does not matter, but each person can belong to only one team.)

The trapezoid $[ABCD]$ has bases $[AB]$ and $[CD]$, with $[AB]$ the longer base. Knowing that $BC=2\,DA$ and that the sum of the angles $\angle DAB$ and $\angle ABC$ is $120^\circ$, determine the angle $\angle DAB$.
How many consecutive zeros are there at the end of the number $2001!=2001\times 2000\times\cdots\times 3\times 2\times 1$?

At a certain moment of a chess game, every row and every column of the board contains an odd number of pieces. Show that the number of pieces standing on black squares is even. (A chessboard has $8$ rows and $8$ columns.)

On a table stand a cone, resting on its base, and six equal spheres tangent to the cone. Moreover, each sphere is tangent to its two neighbouring spheres. Knowing that the radius $R$ of the base of the cone is half its height, determine the radius $r$ of the spheres.
Let $n$ be a positive integer. Show that there is a multiple of $n$ that is written using only the digits $0$ and $1$.

The password Ana Viso chose for her computer consists of the $7$ characters of her name: A, N, A, V, I, S, O. Ordering alphabetically all the different words formed with all these $7$ characters, Ana's password appears in position $881$. What is Ana's password?

Consider five spheres of radius $10$ cm. Four of them are placed on a horizontal table so that their centres form a square of side $20$ cm, and the fifth is placed on top of them so that it touches the other four. What is the distance from the centre of the fifth sphere to the table?

Daniel painted a rectangular board of $2$ metres by $4$ metres with four colours. Knowing that he used more than two colours for the four corners of the board, prove that he painted two points at distance at least $\sqrt5$ metres from each other with the same colour.

The set Blablabla contains all the seven-digit numbers with distinct digits that can be formed with the digits $2,3,4,5,6,7$ and $8$. Show that there are no two numbers in Blablabla such that one of them is divisible by the other.

Consider the three squares shown in the figure: a large square, a small square in one of its corners, and an inclined square whose vertices lie on the four sides of the large square, one side of the inclined square passing through the inner vertex of the small square. Show that if the side lengths of the small square and of the large square are integers, then the area of the small square plus the area of the inclined square is a perfect square.

On 6 March 2002 Coimbra celebrated the 500th anniversary of the birth of the mathematician Pedro Nunes. That morning only ten people entered the bookshop Viva a Ciência. Each of them bought exactly $3$ different books, and any two of them bought at least one copy of a common book. ``The Mathematical Adventures of Pedro Nunes'' was one of the best-selling books that morning. What is the smallest possible number of copies of it that were sold?

The planet Caramelo is a cube with edge $1$ km. The planet is to be wrapped in anti-glutton foam so as to prevent greedy spaceships from coming within $500$ metres of the planet. What is the minimum volume of foam that must surround the planet?

An architect designed a hexagonal column made of $37$ metal tubes of equal thickness, whose cross-section is a regular hexagon with $4$ tubes on each side (tubes arranged in hexagonal packing). Is it possible to build a similar column whose number of tubes ends in $2003$?
Raquel painted $650$ points in a disc of radius $16$ cm. Show that there is an annulus with inner radius $2$ cm and outer radius $3$ cm containing at least $10$ of these points.

In a village there are only $10$ houses, placed around a circular square of radius $r$ metres, each house at the same distance from each of its two nearest houses; label them $A,B,C,\dots,J$ in order around the circle. Every year, on Easter Sunday, the village priest makes the Easter visit, leaving the parish house (point $A$) and following the route of Figure 1: $A,B,C,\dots,J,A$, going each time straight to the next house. This year the priest decided to follow the route of Figure 2: $A,D,G,J,C,F,I,B,E,H,A$, going each time straight to the third house further on. Show that this year the priest will walk $10r$ metres more.

A shepherd left his flock of $k$ sheep to his sons as follows: the eldest received $\left\lfloor\frac k2\right\rfloor$ sheep, the middle one $\left\lfloor\frac k3\right\rfloor$ sheep and the youngest $\left\lfloor\frac k5\right\rfloor$ sheep. Knowing that no sheep was left over, determine all possible values of $k$. (Here $\lfloor x\rfloor$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$.)
Given six irrational numbers, is it always possible to choose three of them such that the sum of any two of these three is irrational?

$2005$ people were in a queue for a Super Rock Pop concert. To give away $3$ backstage passes, the first person in the queue was asked to shout ``Super'', the second ``Rock'', the third ``Pop'', the fourth ``Super'', the fifth ``Rock'', the sixth ``Pop'', and so on. Those who said ``Rock'' or ``Pop'' were eliminated. The process was repeated, always starting from the first person of the new queue, until only $3$ people were left. In which positions were these people at the start?

Triangle $[ABC]$ has a right angle at $A$. The point $D$ lies on side $[BC]$ and the point $E$ on side $[AC]$ so that triangle $[EDC]$ has a right angle at $D$. Show that if $E$ is the midpoint of $[AC]$, then $AB<BD$.

On a board with $a$ rows and $b$ columns, each cell has a switch and a lamp that is off. Pressing the switch of a cell changes the state of the lamp in that cell, together with the lamps in the same row and those in the same column (lamps that are on go off and lamps that are off go on). For which values of $a$ and $b$ is it possible, by pressing a sequence of switches, to end with exactly one lamp on?

A positive integer $n$ is called abundant if the sum of its divisors is greater than $2n$. For example, $18$ is abundant because the sum of its divisors, $1+2+3+6+9+18$, is greater than $36$. Write every even number greater than $46$ as the sum of two abundant numbers.

Consider a quadrilateral $[ABCD]$ that has an inscribed circle and a circumscribed circle. The sides $[AD]$ and $[BC]$ touch the inscribed circle at the points $E$ and $F$ respectively. Show that $$AE\times FC=BF\times ED.$$
Show that there is a unique function $f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$ satisfying $$f(a+b)f(a-b)=f(a^2)$$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb N$ with $a>b$.

Alexandre and Herculano are at Campanhã station waiting for the train. To pass the time, they decide to compute the length of a goods train passing through the station at constant speed. When the front of the train passes them, Alexandre starts walking in the direction of motion of the train and Herculano in the opposite direction. Both walk at the same speed, and each stops at the moment he meets the end of the train. Alexandre walked $45$ metres and Herculano $30$. How long is the train?

In the equilateral triangle $[ABC]$, $D$ is the midpoint of $[AC]$, $E$ is the orthogonal projection of $D$ on $[CB]$, and $F$ is the midpoint of $[DE]$. Prove that $[FB]$ and $[AE]$ are perpendicular.

A bean packing plant has a machine that puts a certain quantity of beans into bags and then a certain number of bags into boxes, which are sent to the customers. One day the machine broke down: the first $n$ bags came out empty, the next $n$ with $1$ bean, the next $n$ with $2$ beans, $\dots$, and the last $n$ with $2006$ beans. To supply each customer with the agreed quantity of bags and beans, the manager wants to distribute the bags over the $2007$ boxes of that day so that all boxes contain the same number of bags and all boxes contain the same number of beans. For which values of $n$ is this possible?
In the parallelogram $[ABCD]$, $E$ is the midpoint of $[AD]$ and $F$ is the orthogonal projection of $B$ on $[CE]$. Prove that triangle $[ABF]$ is isosceles.
Determine all positive integers $n$ such that exactly one fifth of the numbers $1,2,\dots,n$ are divisors of $n$.

The integers from $1$ to $36$ are written on each ticket of the ``Neuro-Millions''. A bet consists of choosing $6$ of these $36$ numbers. Then $6$ numbers between $1$ and $36$ are drawn, forming the winning key. A bet wins a prize if it contains none of the numbers of the key. What is the minimum number of bets needed to guarantee a prize?

João had blue, white and red pearls, and with them he made a necklace of $20$ pearls with as many blue pearls as white ones. João noticed that, however he cut the necklace into two parts each with an even number of pearls, one of the parts always had more blue pearls than white ones. How many red pearls does João's necklace have?
Let $[ABC]$ be a triangle and $X$, $Y$, $Z$ points on the sides $[AB]$, $[BC]$, $[AC]$ respectively. Show that the circles $AXZ$, $BXY$ and $CYZ$ meet at a point.
Determine the largest integer $n$ that is a multiple of all positive integers less than $\sqrt n$.

Fernanda decided to decorate a blanket made of squares with a ribbon and buttons, sewing a button at the centre of each square the ribbon passes through and forming the pattern shown in the figure (the rows of squares are numbered $\dots,-2,-1,0,1,2,\dots$). If Fernanda sews the first button in the shaded square of row $0$, in which row does she sew the $2007$th button?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/pt_2007_p4_fig.png

António's street has $100$ houses numbered from $1$ to $100$. Any house whose number is the difference of the numbers of two houses of the same colour has a different colour. Show that in António's street there are houses of at least five different colours.
In a village the maximum distance between two houses is $M$ and the minimum distance is $m$. Prove that if the village has $6$ houses, then $\frac Mm\ge\sqrt3$.

What is the maximum number of triangles that can be formed with vertices among the points of the figure? (The ten points lie on a square grid: five consecutive points on a horizontal line, one point above each of the first, third and fifth of them, and two points below the third one.)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/pt_2008_p1_fig.png
The triangle $[ABC]$ is inscribed in a circle, $E$ lies on the circle, $D$ lies on the ray $AE$ (beyond $E$), and $\angle CAB=\angle BAE$. Prove that $AB=BD$ if and only if $DE=AC$.

Let $d$ be a positive integer. Given two positive integers $M$ and $N$ with $d$ digits, $M$ is a friend of $N$ if the $d$ numbers obtained by replacing each digit of $M$ by the digit of $N$ in the same position are all multiples of $7$. Determine the values of $d$ for which the following holds: for any two numbers $M$ and $N$ with $d$ digits, if $M$ is a friend of $N$, then $N$ is a friend of $M$.

Nelson challenges Telma to the following game. First Telma removes $2^9$ numbers from the set $\{0,1,2,3,\dots,1024\}$, then Nelson removes $2^8$ of the remaining numbers, then Telma removes $2^7$ numbers, and so on, until only $2$ numbers remain. Nelson must then give Telma, in euros, the difference between these two numbers. What is the largest amount Telma can win regardless of Nelson's strategy?

Let $[ABC]$ be a triangle with a right angle at $A$ and $AB<AC$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $[BC]$ and $D$ the intersection of $[AC]$ with the line through $M$ perpendicular to $[BC]$. Let $E$ be the intersection of the line through $M$ parallel to $[AC]$ with the line through $B$ perpendicular to $[BD]$. Prove that the triangles $[AEM]$ and $[MCA]$ are similar if and only if $\angle ABC=60^\circ$.

Let $n$ be a positive integer greater than $2$. Vanessa has $n$ piles of jade stones, all with different numbers of stones. Vanessa can distribute the stones of any one pile among the other piles so as to obtain $n-1$ piles with equal numbers of stones. She can also distribute the stones of any two piles among the other piles so as to obtain $n-2$ piles with equal numbers of stones. Determine the smallest possible number of jade stones in the largest pile.

A circle was divided into $n$ equal parts. In each of these parts a single number from $1$ to $n$ was placed, in such a way that the distance between consecutive numbers is always the same. The numbers $11$, $4$ and $17$ ended up in consecutive positions. Into how many parts was the circle divided?

Points $N$ and $M$ are marked on the sides $[CD]$ and $[BC]$ of the square $[ABCD]$, respectively. The perimeter of the triangle $[MCN]$ is equal to twice the length of the side of the square. Determine $\angle MAN$.

Duarte wants to draw a square of side $2009$ cm, divided into $2009 \times 2009$ small squares of side $1$ cm, without lifting the pencil. Starting from a corner of the square, what is the length of the shortest line that allows him to make this drawing?
João computed the product of the nonzero digits of each integer from $1$ to $10^{2009}$. Then he added these $10^{2009}$ products. What number did João obtain?

The circles $C_1$ and $C_2$ have different radii and are tangent at the point $T$. Consider arbitrary points $A$ on $C_1$ and $B$ on $C_2$, both different from $T$, such that $\angle BTA = 90^\circ$. What is the locus of the midpoints of the segments $[AB]$ constructed in this way?

Two players play the following game on a circular board with $2009$ cells. The two players alternately place, in an empty cell, one of three pieces, called an explorer ($E$), a trap ($A$) or a stone ($P$). A treasure is a sequence of three consecutive filled cells such that the first one (in either direction) contains an explorer and the middle one does not contain a trap. For example, the sequence $PAE$ is not a treasure, but the sequence $AEE$ is a treasure.

The first player to form a treasure wins. Can one of the players guarantee victory? And, if so, which one?

In the Chapel of Bones there are several candles of the same size. On the first day one candle is lit for one hour. On the second day two candles are lit for one hour, on the third day three candles are lit for one hour, and so on, until the last day, on which all the candles are lit for one hour. At the end of that day, all the candles are completely burnt out. Determine all possibilities for the number of candles.
On a circle, the points $A$ and $B$ lie on opposite arcs determined by the diameter $[CD]$. The segments $[CE]$ and $[DF]$ are perpendicular to $[AB]$. Knowing that $AE = 1$ cm, determine $BF$.

Every day, more than half of the inhabitants of Évora eat sericaia for dessert. Show that there is a group of $10$ inhabitants of Évora such that, in the last $2010$ days, on each day at least one of them ate sericaia for dessert.

Giraldo wrote five distinct natural numbers at the vertices of a pentagon. Then he wrote on each side of the pentagon the least common multiple of the numbers at the two vertices of that side, and noticed that the five numbers he wrote on the sides were equal. What is the smallest number Giraldo may have written on the sides?
Show that every triangle has two sides whose lengths $a$ and $b$ satisfy $$\frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{2} < \frac{a}{b} < \frac{\sqrt{5}+1}{2}.$$

Prove that, for any prime number $p$, it is possible to choose $p$ points of a $p \times p$ grid of points so that no three of the points are collinear. The following figure illustrates a possible choice for $p = 3$ (the chosen points are shown in a different colour).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/portugal_2010_p6_fig.png

A nine-digit telephone number $abcdefghi$ is memorable if the sequence of the first four digits $abcd$ appears in the sequence of the last five digits $efghi$. How many memorable nine-digit numbers are there?

The point $P$, inside the triangle $[ABC]$, lies on the perpendicular bisector of $[AB]$. The points $Q$ and $R$, outside the triangle, are such that $[BPA]$, $[BQC]$ and $[CRA]$ are similar triangles. Show that $[PQCR]$ is a parallelogram.

In a class with $14$ boys, each of them was asked how many classmates had the same first name as him and how many classmates had the same last surname as him. The numbers $0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ and $6$ appeared among the answers. Prove that there are two classmates with the same first name and the same last surname.

Let $[ABC]$ be a triangle, $D$ the orthogonal projection of $B$ onto the bisector of $\angle ACB$, and $E$ the orthogonal projection of $C$ onto the bisector of $\angle ABC$. Prove that the line $DE$ meets the sides $[AB]$ and $[AC]$ at the points of tangency of the incircle of the triangle $[ABC]$.

The number $1000$ can be written as a sum of $16$ consecutive natural numbers: $1000 = 55 + 56 + \dots + 70$. Determine all natural numbers that cannot be written as a sum of two or more consecutive natural numbers.
A five-digit number $abcde$ is called a mountain range if its digits satisfy the inequalities $a < b > c < d > e$. For example, $37452$ is a mountain range. How many mountain ranges are there?

In the triangle $[ABC]$ the bisector of $\angle BAC$ meets $[BC]$ at $D$, and the triangle $[ADC]$ is isosceles with base $[AC]$. Determine the triangle $[ABC]$ with the smallest perimeter, given that the side lengths of the triangles $[ABC]$ and $[DAC]$ are integers.

Helena and Luís are going to play a game with two bags of marbles. They play alternately and each move consists of one of the following:

• removing one marble from one of the bags;
• removing one marble from each of the bags;
• moving one marble from one bag to the other.

The player who leaves both bags empty wins.

Before starting to play, Helena counted the marbles in each bag and said to Luís "You can start!", while thinking "This way I will win for sure!!!".

How could the marbles have been distributed between the bags?
How many integers from $1$ to $1000$ are divisible by the integer part of their cube root?

Isabel has $n$ sheets of paper. She wants to distribute the natural numbers among these sheets, each number being on exactly one sheet. Moreover, whenever two distinct numbers are on the same sheet, their sum must also be on that sheet. Determine the largest number that can be alone on a sheet.

Consider a parallelogram $[ABCD]$ such that the angle $\angle DAB$ is acute. Let $G$ be a point on the line $AB$, distinct from $B$, such that $BC = GC$, and let $H$ be a point on the line $BC$, distinct from $B$, such that $AB = AH$. Prove that the triangle $[GDH]$ is isosceles.

Three holidaymakers, $A$, $B$ and $C$, usually go for a morning run on a beach in Albufeira. On a certain day, they met at a point of the beach and started running at the same time, each at their own pace, which they kept throughout the run. Every time they reached one of the ends of the beach, they reversed direction. No pair of runners ever met at the ends of the beach. At the moment when $A$, $B$ and $C$ were all together again, they decided to end the run. Apart from the initial and final moments, $A$ met $B$ six times and met $C$ eight times. How many times did $B$ and $C$ meet?

In the Republic of Unistan there are $n$ national roads, each connecting exactly two cities, and it is always possible to travel between any two cities along a sequence of roads. The President of Unistan ordered the national roads to be numbered from $1$ to $n$, remembering an old law: whenever a city is served by more than one road, the greatest common divisor of their numbers must be one. Show that it is possible to number the roads without violating the law.
What is the smallest natural number $n$ such that $n!$ has at least $2013$ divisors?

Liliana wants to decorate a rectangular wall made of $m \times n$ tiles. Each tile is square and divided in half by one of its diagonals; one of the halves is painted white and the other black. Liliana does not want two triangles of the same colour to have a side in common. In how many different ways can Liliana decorate the wall?

On each side of a regular polygon with $n$ sides, a point different from the vertices is chosen, giving a new polygon with $n$ sides. For which values of $n$ is it possible that the new polygon is not regular but has all its angles equal?

The ship Meridiano do Bacalhau carries out its fishing campaign over $64$ days. Each day, the captain chooses a direction of navigation, north or south, and the ship sails that day only in that direction. On the first day of the campaign the ship sails $1$ mile, on the second day it sails $2$ miles, and more generally, on day $n$ it sails $n$ miles. At the end of the $64$ days, the ship was $2014$ miles north of the starting point of the campaign. What is the maximum number of days on which the ship may have sailed south?
In the square $[ABCD]$, let $M$ be a point of $[AD]$ and $N$ a point of $[DC]$ such that $\angle BMA = \angle NMD = 60^\circ$. Compute $\angle MBN$.

Amélia and Beatriz play battleship on a square board with $2n$ cells on each side, using very peculiar rules. The game begins with Amélia choosing $n$ rows and $n$ columns of the board, and then placing her $n^2$ submarines in the cells at their intersections.

Then Beatriz chooses a set of cells to torpedo. What is the minimum number of cells Beatriz has to choose to be sure of hitting at least one submarine?
Determine all natural numbers $x$, $y$ and $z$, with $x \le y \le z$, such that $$\left(1+\frac{1}{x}\right)\left(1+\frac{1}{y}\right)\left(1+\frac{1}{z}\right) = 3.$$

In a convex quadrilateral $[ABCD]$ with area $2014$, let $P$ be a point of $[AB]$ and $Q$ a point of $[AD]$ such that each of the triangles $[ABQ]$ and $[ADP]$ has area $1$. Let $R$ be the intersection point of $[AC]$ and $[PQ]$. Determine $\dfrac{RC}{RA}$.

One hundred musicians intend to organise a festival consisting of several concerts. In each concert, while some of the hundred musicians play on stage, the others stay in the audience listening. What is the minimum number of concerts the festival must have so that each of the musicians can hear, from the audience, each of the others performing on stage?

A three-digit number is called firm if it is equal to the product of its units digit by the number formed by the remaining digits. For example, $153$ is firm because $153 = 3 \times 51$.

How many firm numbers are there?
Let $[ABC]$ be a triangle and $D$ a point between $A$ and $B$. If the triangles $[ABC]$, $[ACD]$ and $[BCD]$ are all isosceles, what are the possible values of $\angle ABC$?
The numbers from $1$ to $2015$ are written on sheets of paper in such a way that if $n - m$ is a prime number, then $n$ and $m$ are on different sheets. What is the minimum number of sheets needed?

Let $[ABCD]$ be a parallelogram and $P$ a point between $C$ and $D$. The line parallel to $AD$ through $P$ meets the diagonal $AC$ at $Q$. Knowing that the area of $[PBQ]$ is $2$ and the area of $[ABP]$ is $6$, determine the area of $[PBC]$.

A sequence of integers $(a_0, \dots, a_k)$ is called medalled if, for each $i = 0, \dots, k$, there are exactly $a_i$ elements of the sequence equal to $i$. For example, $(1, 2, 1, 0)$ is medalled.

Find all medalled sequences $(a_0, \dots, a_{2015})$.
For which values of $n$ is it possible to mark $n$ points in the plane so that each point has at least three other points at distance $1$?

To unlock his mobile phone, João slides his finger horizontally or vertically over a numeric grid, similar to the one shown in the figure, describing a $7$-digit code, never passing twice over the same digit. For example, to enter the code $1452369$, João follows the path indicated in the figure.

João has forgotten his code, but he remembers that it is divisible by $9$. How many codes satisfy these conditions?
In how many different ways is it possible to write $2016$ as a sum of a sequence of consecutive natural numbers?

Let $[ABC]$ be an equilateral triangle of side $1$. Determine the length of the shortest segment $[DE]$, where $D$ and $E$ lie on the sides of the triangle, that divides $[ABC]$ into two figures of equal area.

Let $[ABCD]$ be a parallelogram with $AB < BC$ and let $E$, $F$ be points on the circle through $A$, $B$ and $C$ such that $DE$ and $DF$ are tangent to this circle. Knowing that $\angle ADE = \angle CDF$, determine $\angle ABC$.
Determine all natural numbers $x$, $y$ and $z$ such that the number $$2^x + 4^y + 8^z + 16^2$$ is a power of $2$.

The natural numbers are coloured green or blue in such a way that:

• the sum of a green number and a blue number is blue;
• the product of a green number and a blue number is green.

In how many ways can the natural numbers be coloured following these rules, so that $462$ is blue and $2016$ is green?
Determine all integer values of $n$ for which the number $$\frac{14n+25}{2n+1}$$ is a perfect square.

In the triangle $[ABC]$, the bisector of the angle at $C$ and the altitude through $B$ meet at the point $D$. The reflection of the point $D$ in the line $BC$ is a point $E$ lying on the circumcircle of the triangle $[ABC]$. Show that the triangle $[ABC]$ is isosceles.

Five teams take part in an athletics tournament. Each athlete wears a shirt numbered with a positive integer, and all the athletes of the same team have distinct numbers. Each athlete takes part in exactly one event, and in each event exactly one athlete from each team is present. Emídio noticed that the sum of the shirt numbers of the athletes in each event is always $20$. What is the maximum number of athletes in the tournament?

The numbers from $1$ to $8$ are placed at the vertices of a cube, one at each of the eight vertices, in such a way that the sum of the numbers at any three vertices of the same face is greater than $9$. Determine the minimum value that the sum of the numbers of one of the faces can have.

Let $[ABCD]$ be a convex quadrilateral with $AB = 2$, $BC = 3$, $CD = 7$ and $\angle B = 90^\circ$, for which there exists an inscribed circle, that is, a circle tangent to all the sides of the quadrilateral. Determine the radius of this circle.

In a building whose floors are numbered from $1$ to $8$, the builder wants to install lifts in such a way that, for every choice of two floors, there are always at least three lifts that stop at both of these floors. Moreover, each lift can stop at no more than $5$ floors.

What is the minimum number of lifts that must be installed?

Artur thought of a positive integer and noticed that the sum of its three smallest divisors is $17$ and that the sum of its three largest divisors is $3905$. Find all the numbers Artur may have thought of.

In the figure, $[ABCD]$ is a square of side $1$. The points $E$, $F$, $G$ and $H$ are such that $[AFB]$, $[BGC]$, $[CHD]$ and $[DEA]$ are right triangles. Let $[ABC]$ be any triangle and let $D$, $E$ and $F$ be the reflections of the circumcentre in the three sides. Show that the triangles $[ABC]$ and $[DEF]$ are congruent.

A museum wants to protect its most valuable piece by keeping it under constant surveillance. To do so, it wants to have guards watching the piece, in shifts of $7$ consecutive hours. Each guard starts his shift at the same time every day. A guard is indispensable if there is some moment of the day at which he is alone watching the piece. Find all possibilities for the number of guards watching the piece such that all of them are indispensable.

A five-digit integer is called balanced if the sum of any three of its digits is divisible by each of the other two. How many balanced numbers are there?

The factorial of a natural number $n$, denoted by $n!$, is the product of all positive integers less than or equal to $n$, that is, $$1 \times 2 \times \dots \times (n-1) \times n.$$ Determine all natural numbers $n$ for which it is possible to replace, in the above expression, one or more factors $k$ by $k!$ so that the result is a perfect square.

On a board with $3$ columns and $4$ rows, each of the $12$ squares is to be painted green or white. In the first and the last row, the number of squares painted green must be equal. Moreover, in the first and the last column, the number of squares painted green must also be equal. In how many different ways can the board be painted?

Let $[ABC]$ be an acute triangle and $\Gamma$ its circumcircle. Let $D$ be the point on the line $AB$ such that $A$ is the midpoint of the segment $[DB]$, and let $P$ be the intersection point of $CD$ with $\Gamma$. The points $W$ and $L$ lie on the minor arcs $BC$ and $AB$, respectively, and are such that the arcs $BW$, $LA$ and $AP$ are equal. The lines $LC$ and $AW$ meet at $Q$. Show that $LQ = BQ$.

A metro network with $n \ge 2$ stations, in which each station is connected to each of the others by a one-way line, is called dispersed if there are two stations $A$ and $B$ such that it is not possible to go from $A$ to $B$ using the network.

If a network is dispersed, but it is possible to choose a station $A$ and reverse the direction of all the lines to and from $A$ so that the new network is no longer dispersed, the network is called correctable.

Find all integers $n$ for which there exists a network with $n$ stations that is dispersed and not correctable.

A positive integer $n$ is called GOOD if there exists a permutation $(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n)$ of the integers from $1$ to $n$ such that, for every $k$, $k + a_k$ is a perfect square. For example, $5$ is a GOOD number, since the permutation $(3, 2, 1, 5, 4)$ satisfies the condition: $1+3 = 2^2$, $2+2 = 2^2$, $3+1 = 2^2$, $4+5 = 3^2$ and $5+4 = 3^2$.

Find all GOOD numbers up to $12$.

In a triangle $[ABC]$, the angle at $C$ is twice the angle at $A$. A point $D$ is marked on the side $[AC]$ such that $\angle ABD = \angle DBC$. Knowing that $AB = 10$ and $CD = 3$, what is the length of the side $[BC]$?

Given a subset of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$, we define its alternating sum as follows: we arrange the elements of the subset in decreasing order and, starting with the largest, alternately add and subtract the successive numbers. For example, the alternating sum of the set $\{1, 3, 4, 6, 8\}$ is $8 - 6 + 4 - 3 + 1 = 4$.

Determine the sum of the alternating sums of all subsets of $\{1, 2, \dots, 10\}$ with an odd number of elements.
Determine the sum of all fractions of the form $\dfrac{1}{ab}$, where $0 < a < b \le 200$ are coprime natural numbers such that $a + b > 200$.

Joana divided $365$ by every integer from $1$ to $365$ and added up all the remainders. Then she divided $366$ by every integer from $1$ to $366$ and also added up all the remainders. Which of the two sums is larger, and what is the difference between them?
Let $[ABC]$ be a triangle such that $AB = AC$. Let $D$ be a point on $[BC]$ and $E$ a point on $[AD]$ such that $\angle BED = \angle BAC = 2\angle DEC$. Show that $DB = 2\,CD$.
Consider all sequences of $k$ elements $(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_k)$, where each $a_i$ belongs to the set $\{1, 2, \dots, 2021\}$. What is the sum of the smallest elements of all these sequences?

Pedro and Tiago are going to play a game with a deck of $n$ cards, numbered from $1$ to $n$.

Starting with Pedro, they take cards alternately and receive the number of points shown on the card. However, whenever a player takes the card with the largest number among those remaining in the deck, he must skip his next turn, not taking any card. When the deck runs out, the player with more points wins.

Knowing that Tiago can at least draw, regardless of Pedro's moves, how many cards does the deck have? Find all possibilities.

Raul's class has $15$ students, all of different heights. In how many different ways can this line be formed?

Proença has a new $8 \times 8$ chessboard and wants to decompose it into $n$ non-overlapping rectangles such that:

(i) each rectangle has as many white squares as black squares;
(ii) no two rectangles have the same number of squares.

Determine the maximum value of $n$ for which such a decomposition is possible.

For this value of $n$, determine all possible sets $\{A_1, \dots, A_n\}$, where $A_i$ is the number of squares of rectangle $i$, for which a decomposition of the board under the required conditions is possible.
Let $[AD]$ be a median of the triangle $[ABC]$. Knowing that $\angle ADB = 45^\circ$ and $\angle ACB = 30^\circ$, show that $\angle BAD = 30^\circ$.

In a badminton competition there are $16$ players, of whom $10$ are professionals and $6$ are amateurs. In a first stage, eight matches are drawn. Among the eight winners of these matches, four matches are drawn. The four winners qualify for the semi-finals of the competition.

Assuming that whenever a professional and an amateur play each other the professional wins, what is the probability that an amateur player reaches the semi-finals of the competition?

Given two natural numbers $a < b$, Xavier and Zé play the following game.

First, Xavier writes $a$ consecutive numbers of his choice; then he repeats some of them, also of his choice, until he has $b$ numbers, with the condition that the sum of the $b$ numbers written is even.

Zé wins the game if he manages to split the numbers into two groups with the same sum. Otherwise, Xavier wins.

For example, for $a = 4$ and $b = 7$, if Xavier wrote the numbers $3, 4, 5, 6, 3, 3, 4$, Zé could win by splitting these numbers into the groups $3, 3, 4, 4$ and $3, 5, 6$.

For which values of $a$ and $b$ can Xavier guarantee victory?

Ana, Bruno and Carolina played table tennis among themselves. In each match only two of the friends played, the third one resting. Each time one of the friends won a match, he or she rested during the following match. Ana played $12$ matches, Bruno played $21$ matches and Carolina rested during $8$ matches.

Who rested in the last match?

Let $[AB]$ be a diameter of a circle with centre $O$ and radius $1$. Let $P$ be a point on the circle different from $A$ and $B$, and let $Q$ be the midpoint of the arc $AP$. The line through $O$ parallel to $PQ$ meets the line $PB$ at the point $S$.

Determine $PS$.

A box with a $4 \times 2$ base and height $2$ is open at the top. Tomás wants to fill the box completely with some of his cubes. He has $16$ identical cubes of volume $1$ and two identical cubes of volume $8$. A cube of volume $1$ can only be placed in the upper layer if the cube of the lower layer below it has already been placed.

In how many ways can Tomás fill the box with cubes, placing them one at a time?

Let $[ABC]$ be an equilateral triangle and $P$ a point of $AC$ such that $PC = 7$. The line through $P$ perpendicular to $AC$ meets $CB$ at the point $M$ and meets $AB$ at the point $Q$. The midpoint $N$ of $[MQ]$ is such that $BN = 14$.

Determine the side of the triangle $[ABC]$.

In the village of numbers, the houses are numbered from $1$ to $n$. Meanwhile, one of the houses was demolished. Duarte computed that the average of the numbers of the houses that still exist is $\frac{202}{3}$. How many houses were there in the village and what is the number of the demolished house?

A rectangular board, with a symbol in each cell, is called magnificent if, for each row $L$ and each pair of columns $C$ and $D$, there is another row $M$ in the board exactly equal to $L$, except in the columns $C$ and $D$, where $M$ has symbols different from those of $L$.

What is the smallest possible number of rows of a magnificent board with $2023$ columns?
A positive integer is called scalabitan if the sum of its digits is a multiple of $17$ and the sum of the digits of its successor is also a multiple of $17$. What is the smallest scalabitan number?

Consider a triangle $[ABC]$. The midpoints of $[BC]$, $[CA]$ and $[AB]$ are $D$, $E$ and $F$, respectively. The medians $[AD]$ and $[BE]$ are perpendicular, with $AD = 12$ and $BE = 9$. What is the length of $[CF]$?
Consider sequences of $0$'s and $1$'s in which there are at most two consecutive zeros. How many such sequences of length $10$ are there?

The circle inscribed in the square $[ABCD]$, of side $10$ cm, meets the sides $[BC]$ and $[AD]$ at the points $M$ and $N$, respectively. The point $I$ is the intersection point of $[AM]$ with the circle, different from $M$, and $P$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $I$ to $MN$. Determine $PI$.

Ten teams take part in a sports championship, five Portuguese and five Spanish. Each team plays against four different teams: one home game and one away game against Portuguese teams; and one home game and one away game against Spanish teams.

In how many different ways is it possible to choose the games of this championship?

The player who leaves the bag empty wins.

For each value of $n$, who has a winning strategy, that is, who can guarantee winning the game regardless of the other player's moves?

The convex quadrilateral $[ABCD]$ has acute interior angles at $A$ and $D$, and $AB = BC = CD$. Knowing that $\angle BDA = 30^\circ$, show that $\angle DAC = 30^\circ$.

A computer science teacher asked his students to write a program that, given a list of $n$ numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$, computes the list $b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n$, where $b_k$ is the number of times the number $a_k$ appears in the list. Maria wants to solve a challenge with a deck of cards, each with a different picture. Initially, the cards are randomly distributed into two piles, not necessarily of equal size. Maria's goal is to move all the cards into the same pile.

In each move, Maria takes the top card of each pile and confronts them. In the rule book there is a table that indicates, for each confrontation of cards, which of the two wins. Show that it is always possible for Maria to solve the challenge, regardless of the initial distribution of the cards and of the table in the rule book.
